component.name: Apache Grails
component.description: Opinionated, full-stack web application framework for the JVM composing Apache Groovy, Spring Framework, Spring Boot, GORM data mapping, and GSP/JSON view rendering, plus CLI tools and the separately operated grails-forge application generator. Grails is embedded into a user-authored web application; the unit of trust modeled is an application using the Grails framework, not a Grails server. The threat model is versioned against the 8.0.x branch and is a draft not yet ratified by maintainers.

externalReferences.comment: Source security model document; this file is a structured translation of it.

blueprints.name: Grails application
blueprints.description: The principal trust boundary is the HTTP request boundary: data crossing from an untrusted end user into the application's controller layer at GrailsDispatcherServlet, where request parameters, headers, cookies, and bodies are treated as attacker-controlled. A secondary boundary is the filesystem/environment boundary at application startup, where configuration is loaded; the framework's most powerful capabilities (Groovy DSL evaluation, classloader injection) are guarded by the assumption that code on the classpath is trusted.

assets.name: HTTP request ingress
assets.description: GrailsDispatcherServlet, UrlMappingsHandlerMapping, and interceptors, receiving requests from the Spring Boot embedded container.

assets.name: Data binding (GrailsWebDataBinder)
assets.description: Binds request parameters and bodies to command objects and domain classes; identified as the highest-risk surface. Collection growth is capped by autoGrowCollectionLimit (default 256) and multipart uploads by maxFileSize/maxRequestSize (128000 bytes each by default).

assets.name: View rendering and codecs
assets.description: GSP, JSON, and Markup views plus the grails-encoder codec subsystem (HTMLCodec, URLCodec, JavaScriptCodec, Base64Codec); the output-side trust transition, encoding data per the view's content type.

assets.name: GORM mapping and validation integration
assets.description: Data mapping to Hibernate/MongoDB/Neo4j; parameterized queries and the criteria/where DSL escape values safely, while HQL string concatenation is the canonical risk path.

assets.name: Configuration loading and plugin discovery
assets.description: Loads application.yml and application.groovy (evaluated as Groovy), external config from grails.config.locations, and plugins/artefacts from the classpath at startup; all are trusted operator/developer inputs.

assets.name: CLI and shell (grails-shell-cli)
assets.description: Developer-run tooling that downloads profile JARs via Maven resolution and executes their Groovy command scripts; end users do not invoke it.

zones.name: End users (HTTP clients)
zones.description: Remote, unauthenticated HTTP clients; the source of all attacker-controllable input considered in the model.

zones.name: Grails application process
zones.description: Framework, developer-authored code, and plugins running with full application privileges; no sandbox or isolation between them.

zones.name: Host environment
zones.description: Filesystem, classpath, environment variables, and system properties controlled by the trusted operator and developer.

persona.description: Untrusted. Sends HTTP requests to a deployed Grails application; crafts arbitrary headers, cookies, parameters, JSON/XML bodies, and multipart uploads up to operator-configured limits, and may enumerate URL spaces including guessable IDs. You must assume that every unprotected URL is publicly accessible one way or another.
Trusted. Writes controllers, services, domain classes, URL mappings, and GSP templates; configures application.yml/application.groovy; runs the CLI; chooses plugins.
Trusted-by-association. Code from a third-party plugin or profile runs with full application privileges; the framework does not isolate plugin code.

assumptions.description: JDK 21 or higher, Apache Groovy 4.0.x, Spring Boot 4.0.x / Spring Framework 7.0.x, Jakarta EE 10 servlet API.
The application is deployed by a trusted operator on hardware and OS the operator controls; transport security (TLS) is provided by the embedded container or a fronting reverse proxy.

The application classpath contains only artifacts the operator or developer chose; plugin code, application.groovy, doWithSpring closures, AST transforms, and every JAR on the classpath are fully trusted and execute with application privileges, with no sandbox or provenance verification beyond Maven resolution.
Thread-per-request servlet model with one logical request per thread, and one application per JVM; no cross-process or cross-tenant isolation is assumed.

Environment variables and system properties consulted at startup (GRAILS_ENV, grails.env, grails.config.locations, and the standard Spring Boot set) reflect operator intent; deployments use GRAILS_ENV=production, since development mode loosens stack-trace exposure and dev-tool behavior.

threats.name: SQL/HQL injection through GORM queries
threats.description: Parameterized GORM queries (named or positional parameters, criteria DSL, where DSL with bound values) are claimed to be SQL/HQL-injection safe; a violation (attacker-controlled data appearing unescaped in executed SQL) is security-critical and CVE-eligible. Queries built by string concatenation, such as Book.find with GString interpolation of params, are documented as unsafe and are the developer's responsibility.

threats.name: Bypass of default output encoding (XSS and URL injection)
threats.description: Default GSP expression output is HTML-encoded, Grails-supplied link/form tag helpers URL-encode their parameter values, and the codecs (HTMLCodec, URLCodec, JavaScriptCodec, Base64Codec) encode for their stated context; violations of any of these are security-critical and CVE-eligible. XSS in templates rendered with the codec disabled (grails.views.default.codec=none) or values explicitly passed through raw() is disclaimed: the opt-out is the developer's stated intent, and reports requiring non-default codec settings are out of model.

threats.name: CSRF against forms using the synchronizer token
threats.description: A form rendered with useToken="true" whose receiving action uses withForm blocks naive CSRF and double-submit; token validation accepting a missing, reused, or attacker-supplied token is security-critical. CSRF protection for requests not protected by useToken is disclaimed: useToken is opt-in per form, and state-mutating actions without it are not CSRF-protected by the framework.

threats.name: Mass assignment through data binding
threats.description: Data binding is claimed to respect bindable=false and explicit include/exclude lists; a field marked unbindable being set from request input is security-critical. Binding the request map directly to a domain class (new DomainClass(params), properties = params) without an allow-list is a known misuse pattern that lets the request set fields the developer never intended, including id, version, role booleans, and association references.

threats.name: Resource exhaustion through data binding limits
threats.description: maxFileSize, maxRequestSize, and autoGrowCollectionLimit provide bounded data-binding memory when the operator does not raise them past application needs; memory growth proportional to attacker input regardless of the limit is a bug. Hangs or unbounded memory growth driven by bounded request input is a bug; super-linear CPU in unbounded developer-authored regex (ReDoS in URL mappings or constraint regexes) is a developer responsibility, and slow-but-completes is not a framework bug at any input size.

threats.name: Missing authentication, authorization, and session management
threats.description: The framework ships no built-in user store, login flow, or session-based auth; authentication, authorization, session management, and password storage are disclaimed by design and delegated to the Spring Security plugin, Apache Shiro, or an equivalent. @Secured annotations are integration-shaped sugar for the Spring Security plugin and are inert without it.

threats.name: Unauthorized domain-object access via guessable IDs
threats.description: The framework does not check that the requesting user is permitted to view the object identified by params.id; authorization for individual domain-object access is disclaimed and must be enforced by the developer against the authenticated principal.

threats.name: Open redirect from request-derived targets
threats.description: Using a request parameter as a redirect target (redirect(url: params.next)) is a documented misuse pattern and open-redirect/phishing pivot; the framework will not add an allow-list to redirect() itself.

threats.name: Groovy code execution via trusted configuration and classpath
threats.description: application.groovy, grails.config.locations targets, domain mapping closures, Liquibase Groovy change logs, and every JAR on the classpath are evaluated or executed with full application privileges; Groovy on the classpath is trusted, full stop, with no sandbox. Reports requiring attacker control of these surfaces are out of model as trusted input; pointing grails.config.locations at attacker-writable storage is equivalent to classpath compromise and is the operator's mistake.

threats.name: Exposure of interactive consoles
threats.description: The interactive consoles (GrailsShell, GroovyConsole) provide arbitrary Groovy code execution with full application-context access by design; they are developer-only tools, and reachability from a deployed application is a deployment-configuration finding against the operator, not a framework vulnerability.

threats.name: Denial of service by request volume
threats.description: Rate limiting and DoS protection against request volume are disclaimed: there is no built-in throttling; operators must add it at the proxy or via Spring Security or bucket4j, and developers must sanitize and bound parameters that size query results (max, offset).

threats.name: Supply-chain compromise of CLI profiles and plugins
threats.description: The CLI downloads profile JARs via standard Maven resolution and executes their Groovy command scripts; the framework does not verify provenance beyond what Maven Resolver provides, and trust in the configured repository is operator-supplied. A typosquat or repository compromise, and compromised plugins on the classpath generally, are operator/developer responsibility and out of scope, as is the build-time supply chain.

threats.name: Well-known attack classes the framework does not defend against
threats.description: One sentence per class in the source document: SSRF (no built-in URL-fetch allow-list), XXE in XML data binding (parser's responsibility), ReDoS in developer-authored URL mappings and constraint regexes, zip-bomb/archive expansion, path traversal through MultipartFile.originalFilename used as a filesystem path, JSON/XML DoS via deep nesting, session fixation/replay/sidejacking (auth plugin's responsibility), and cache-key poisoning in Spring Boot caching layers. Constant-time cryptographic operations are also not provided.

trustBoundaries.name: HTTP request trust boundary
trustBoundaries.description: The trust transition occurs at GrailsDispatcherServlet: request parameters, headers, cookies, and request bodies are treated as attacker-controlled within the framework, and the output codec layer is the matching transition on the response side.

trustBoundaries.name: Startup configuration trust boundary
trustBoundaries.description: Configuration loading and plugin discovery are reachable only with control of grails.config.locations, environment variables, or the classpath, all of which require local privilege at or above the application process; code and configuration crossing this boundary are trusted by design.

controls.name: Parameterized GORM queries
controls.description: Named or positional parameters, the criteria DSL, and the where DSL with bound values are injection-safe; developers must never concatenate request parameters into HQL/SQL/JPQL/Groovy strings.

controls.name: Default output encoding and codecs
controls.description: GSP expression and scriptlet contexts default to the html codec (XSS protection on by default), tag helpers URL-encode parameter values, and the codec subsystem encodes for each stated context. Keep grails.views.default.codec and the GSP context codecs at their HTML-encoding defaults; setting them to none disables automatic output encoding.

controls.name: Synchronizer token (useToken / withForm)
controls.description: Apply useToken (or equivalent CSRF protection from the auth plugin) on every state-mutating form, handled with withForm. It blocks naive cross-site form submissions and accidental double-submits; it is not a replay-protection mechanism.

controls.name: Binding allow-lists (bindable, include/exclude, command objects)
controls.description: Data binding respects bindable=false and explicit include/exclude lists across bindData, command-object binding, domain-class constructor binding, and properties assignment. Bind request data through command objects or explicit allow-lists, never by passing params directly into a domain class. bindable=false is not an access control or validation constraint: it only prevents setting from request-binding sources.

controls.name: Bounded data-binding resources
controls.description: autoGrowCollectionLimit defaults to 256, capping automatic collection growth from deeply indexed parameters; grails.controllers.upload.maxFileSize and maxRequestSize default to 128000 bytes each. Operators who raise these past application needs expose themselves to DoS.

controls.name: Use a real authentication and authorization layer
controls.description: Integrate the Spring Security plugin, Apache Shiro, or an equivalent; the framework provides no replacement for authentication, authorization, or session management.

controls.name: Authorize every domain-object access by ID
controls.description: Authorize each loaded object against the authenticated principal (via ACL support, a per-action interceptor, or an explicit ownership check) before returning, rendering, or mutating it; never rely on guessable IDs as an access control.

controls.name: Allow-list redirect targets
controls.description: Never use a request parameter as a redirect target without an allow-list of permitted destinations.

controls.name: Protect configuration and code sources
controls.description: Treat application.groovy, plugin doWithSpring blocks, and all classpath code as part of the trusted computing base; source grails.config.locations only from trusted operator-controlled paths (never user input or attacker-writable storage such as world-writable directories or unprotected buckets); keep Liquibase Groovy change logs in the versioned source tree; and deploy with GRAILS_ENV=production.

controls.name: Keep interactive consoles off the network
controls.description: Bind GrailsShell, GroovyConsole, and any Groovy-evaluating actuator endpoint to localhost or disable them in production; do not expose grails-console artefacts through the embedded container.

controls.name: Rate limiting at the proxy
controls.description: Cap request rate at the proxy or via Spring Security or bucket4j, cap multipart upload size at the application boundary, and sanitize any request parameter used to size query results.

controls.name: Validate multipart uploads
controls.description: Validate MultipartFile.originalFilename and contentType before use; never use the original filename as a filesystem path, and verify content type server-side against the actual bytes.
